draft.title: Moving plates
card: Earth's outer layer of rock is called the crust. It is broken into large pieces called plates, which fit together like a cracked eggshell.
The plates move very slowly, only a few centimetres each year. They are carried on the hotter rock beneath them.
Plates can pull apart, which can make new crust. They can push together, which can build mountains. They can slide past each other.
The action where plates meet can cause earthquakes. Pulling apart and pushing together can also cause volcanoes.
draft.remember: Plates move slowly, and the action at their edges can cause earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.

a.q: Which statement best describes Earth's plates?
opts: Pieces of crust that move slowly over time
Pieces of crust that are fixed in place
Pieces of crust that move a few metres a day
Pieces of crust that float only in the oceans
a.why: The crust is broken into plates that move a few centimetres each year. They are not fixed, and they are far too slow to move metres in a day.
a.clue: Think about how fast and how far plates move.

b.q: Two plates near the coast of a country are pushing towards each other. Which result is most likely over millions of years?
opts: A mountain range slowly builds up
The two plates become one fixed plate
A wide new ocean opens between them
The plates stop moving and earthquakes end
b.why: Plates that push together can build mountains. A new ocean opens where plates pull apart, which is the opposite movement. Plates keep moving, so earthquakes do not end.
b.clue: Pushing together is the opposite of pulling apart.

wants.brief: A simple world map showing Earth's crust divided into plates, with the plate boundaries drawn as lines and arrows showing the direction each plate moves.
wants.why: It shows that the crust is broken into plates that move.

a.best: Pieces of crust that move slowly over time

b.best: A mountain range slowly builds up
